title: For us one God and one Lord
source_text: Τοιαῦτα καὶ περὶ κυρίου καὶ κυρίων διδάσκουσιν ἡμᾶς ἐξετάζειν καὶ φρονεῖν οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι, ὅπου μὲν λέγοντες· „ἐξομολογεῖσθε τῷ θεῷ τῶν θεῶν, ὅτι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ· ἐξομολογεῖσθε τῷ κυρίῳ τῶν κυρίων, ὅτι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ,“ ὅπου δὲ ὅτι ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς „βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων.“ οἶδε δὲ ὁ λόγος θεοὺς τοὺς μέν τινας λεγομένους τοὺς δὲ καὶ ὄντας, εἴτε λεγομένους εἴτε μή· τὸ δ᾿ αὐτὸ διδάσκων καὶ περὶ κυρίων τῶν ὄντων καὶ μὴ λέγει ὁ Παῦλος· „καὶ γὰρ εἴπερ εἰσὶ λεγόμενοι θεοὶ εἴτ᾿ ἐν οὐρανῷ εἴτ᾿ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὥσπερ εἰσὶ θεοὶ πολλοὶ καὶ κύριοι πολλοί.“ εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ „ὁ τῶν. θεῶν θεὸς“ καλεῖ „ἀπ᾿ ἀνατολῶν“ καὶ „δυσμῶν“ ἐπὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μερίδα διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ οὓς βούλεται, κύριος δὲ ὢν ὁ Χριστὸς τοῦ θεοῦ δείκνυσιν δι᾿ ὧν ἐπέβη τοῖς πάντων ὁρίοις καὶ πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀπὸ πάντων ὁρίων καλεῖ ὅτι ἐστὶ πάντων τῶν κυριευόντων διαφέρων· διὰ τοῦτο ταῦτ᾿ ἐπιστάμενος ὁ Παῦλός φησι μεθ᾿ ἃ παρεθέμην· „ἀλλ᾿ ἡμῖν εἷς θεὸς ὁ πατὴρ, ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ εἷς κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, δι᾿ οὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ ἡμεῖς δι᾿ αὐτοῦ.“ θεωρῶν τε θαυμάσιόν τινα καὶ μυστηριώδη λόγον κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἐπιφέρει αὐτοῖς· „ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἐν πᾶσιν ἡ γνῶσις.“ ἐπὰν δὲ λέγῃ· „ἀλλ᾿ ἡμῖν εἷς θεὸς ὁ πατὴρ, ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ εἷς κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, δι᾿ οὗ τὰ πάντα,“ τὸ „ἡμῖν“ λέγει ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ καὶ πάντων τῶν ἀναβεβηκότων πρὸς τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν „τῶν θεῶν“ καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι κύριον „τῶν κυρίων.“ ἀναβέβηκε δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν ὁ ἀσχίστως καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀμερίστως αὐτὸν σέβων διὰ τοῦ μόνου προσάγοντος ἐκείνῳ υἱοῦ, τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου καὶ σοφίας ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ θεωρουμένου, τοὺς παντὶ τρόπῳ πειρωμένους ἑαυτοὺς οἰκειῶσαι δι᾿ ἐξαιρέτων λόγων καὶ πράξεων καὶ διανοημάτων [καὶ νοημάτων] τῷ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργῷ θεῷ. παρὰ ταῦτα δ᾿ οἶμαι καὶ τὰ τούτοις παραπλήσια τὸν μετασχηματιζόμενον „εἰς ἄγγελον φωτὸς“ ἄρχοντα „τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου“ πεποιηκέναι τὸ „τῷ δὲ ἕπεται στρατιὰ θεῶν τε καὶ δαιμόνων, κατὰ ἕνδεκα μοίρας τεταγμένη.“ ἐν οἷς περὶ ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τῶν φιλοσοφησάντων λέγει τό· „μετὰ μὲν Διὸς ἡμεῖς, ἄλλοι δὲ μετὰ ἄλλων δαιμόνων.“
pass_a_gloss: Such things also about Lord and lords the divine words (θεῖοι λόγοι) teach us to examine (ἐξετάζω) and to think (φρονέω), in one place saying 'confess/give thanks (ἐξομολογέομαι) to the God of the gods, for his mercy (ἔλεος) is for the age; give thanks to the Lord of the lords, for his mercy is for the age', in another that God is 'King of those reigning (βασιλεύω) and Lord of those exercising lordship (κυριεύω)'. The word knows gods, some called (λεγόμενοι), others also being (ὄντες), whether called or not; teaching the same about lords who are and are not, Paul says 'for even if there are so-called gods whether in heaven or upon the earth, as there are many gods and many lords'. Then since 'the God of the gods' calls 'from the east' and 'west' to his own portion (μερίς) through Jesus whom he wills, and the Christ of God, being Lord, shows, through the things by which he set foot on (ἐπιβαίνω) the borders (ὅριον) of all and calls to himself from all borders, that he is surpassing (διαφέρω) all those exercising lordship; for this reason, knowing these things, Paul says after what I set out (παρατίθημι): 'but for us one God the Father, from whom all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things, and we through him'. And beholding (θεωρέω) a wonderful (θαυμάσιος) and mysterious (μυστηριώδης) word in the place, he adds to them 'but not in all is the knowledge (γνῶσις)'. When he says 'but for us ...', he says 'for us' of himself and all those having ascended (ἀναβαίνω) to the God over all 'of the gods' and to the Lord over all 'of the lords'. He has ascended to the God over all who worships (σέβω) him unsplit (ἀσχίστως), undivided (ἀδιαιρέτως), unparted (ἀμερίστως), through the only one bringing to (προσάγω) him, the Son, God's Word and Wisdom (σοφία) beheld in Jesus, those trying in every way to make themselves akin (οἰκειόω) through excellent (ἐξαίρετος) words and deeds (πρᾶξις) and thoughts (διανόημα) to the God, craftsman (δημιουργός) of the all. Beside these and the things near these I think the ruler (ἄρχων) 'of this age (αἰών)' transforming himself (μετασχηματίζομαι) 'into an angel of light' has made (ποιέω) the 'and him follows (ἕπομαι) an army (στρατιά) of gods and demons, ordered (τάσσω) according to eleven portions (μοῖρα)'; in which about himself and those having philosophised (φιλοσοφέω) he says 'with Zeus we, others with other demons'.
pass_b_english: Such, too, are the things that the divine words teach us to examine and to hold about the Lord and lords. In one place they say: “Give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy is for ever; give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy is for ever” (Psalm 136:2–3); in another, that God is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). The word knows of gods, some of whom are so called, while others actually are gods, whether they are so called or not. Paul teaches the same about lords too, both those who are and those who are not, when he says: “For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5).

Then, since “the God of gods” calls “from the east” and “the west” (Psalm 50:1; Matthew 8:11) into His own portion, through Jesus, those whom He wills, and since the Christ of God, being Lord, shows that He surpasses all who hold lordship by the very fact that He has set foot within the borders of all and calls to Himself from every border, for this reason Paul, knowing these things, says after the words I have quoted: “yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through Him” (1 Corinthians 8:6). And seeing a wonderful and mysterious teaching in the passage, he adds to these words: “But not all have this knowledge” (1 Corinthians 8:7).

When he says, “yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6), he says “for us” of himself and of all who have ascended to the God over all, the God “of gods,” and to the Lord over all, the Lord “of lords.” And the one who has ascended to the God over all is he who worships Him without division, without separation, without partition, through the Son, God’s Word and Wisdom seen in Jesus, who alone brings to Him those who try in every way, by excellent words and deeds and thoughts, to bring themselves into kinship with God, the Maker of the universe.

Over against these truths, and others like them, I think that the ruler “of this age” (1 Corinthians 2:6), who disguises himself “as an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14), produced the saying: “And there follows him a host of gods and demons, marshalled in eleven companies” (Plato, Phaedrus 246e). In this passage he says of himself and of those who have practised philosophy: “We with Zeus, and others with other demons” (Plato, Phaedrus 250b).

choices.choice: Psalm 136:2-3 = LXX 135:2-3. Psalm 50:1 = LXX 49:1 (‘from the rising of the sun to its setting’), echoed here by ‘from the east and the west’; the exact pair ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν καὶ δυσμῶν, with calling into the Kingdom, is Matthew 8:11 (compare Luke 13:29), so both are cited. LXX ἐξομολογεῖσθε ... ὅτι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ has no verb in the last clause: rendered ‘His mercy is for ever’. 1 Timothy 6:15 reads exactly βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων; rendered with the familiar ‘King of kings and Lord of lords’. ‘the ruler of this age’: ἄρχοντα τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου echoes 1 Corinthians 2:6, 8 (τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου); compare 2 Corinthians 4:4 and John 12:31. Uncited allusions: ‘His own portion’ (μερίς) recalls Deuteronomy 32:9; ‘the Christ of God’ is Luke 9:20’s phrase; ‘the only one who brings to Him’ recalls 1 Peter 3:18 (προσαγάγῃ τῷ θεῷ) and John 14:6; ‘Word and Wisdom’ recalls John 1:1 and 1 Corinthians 1:24. [καὶ νοημάτων] is bracketed for deletion by Koetschau and left untranslated. The Plato quotations differ from the received Phaedrus text: 246e has κατὰ ἕνδεκα μέρη κεκοσμημένη (Origen κατὰ ἕνδεκα μοίρας τεταγμένη), and 250b has μετ᾽ ἄλλου θεῶν (Origen μετὰ ἄλλων δαιμόνων); translated as Origen quotes them. ‘he says of himself’: the subject of λέγει is the speaker of the Phaedrus passage (Plato, through Socrates); kept as ‘he’ as in the Greek. The θεοὶ λεγόμενοι / ὄντες distinction is rendered ‘so called’ / ‘actually are gods’ (καὶ ὄντας). παρὰ ταῦτα ... πεποιηκέναι: παρά with the accusative read as ‘over against’ (the devil’s counterfeit set beside the true teaching); ‘besides these’ is possible. The sentence on the one who has ascended is reordered for English: Greek has ὁ ... σέβων as subject, then the Son ‘who alone brings’ τοὺς ... πειρωμένους as object of προσάγοντος.
